output.answer: RLHF assistants face a tension between complying with harmful requests when optimized for helpfulness and becoming evasive when optimized for harmlessness; refusals can persist even beyond the objectionable question. Researchers reduced this conflict by mixing helpfulness and harmlessness preference data, with larger preference models handling both objectives more successfully. Constitutional AI trained on constitution-guided critiques and revised responses, then combined AI-generated harmlessness preferences with human helpfulness feedback to encourage engagement and explained refusals. In its evaluations, Constitutional AI models were less harmful at a given level of helpfulness than the human-feedback baselines. Sparrow used targeted human judgements of specific rules alongside response preferences in multi-objective RLHF, improving preference ratings and resistance to adversarial probing, although rule violations remained.

claims.text: Helpfulness optimization can encourage harmful compliance, while harmlessness optimization can produce evasiveness and lower helpfulness.
claims.quote: That is, helpfulness tends to increase harmfulness, since models are willing to obey pernicious requests, and conversely models trained to be harmless tend to be more evasive and generally less helpful.

claims.text: The earlier helpful-and-harmless assistant could remain evasive throughout a conversation because human feedback rewarded evasiveness on harmful inputs.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, once it encountered objectionable queries, it
could get stuck producing evasive responses4 for the remainder of the conversation. Ultimately this was due
to the fact that evasiveness was rewarded as a response to harmful inputs by our crowdworkers.

claims.text: Mixing helpfulness and harmlessness preference data allowed preference models to encourage appropriate assistance and refusal of harmful requests.
claims.quote:
Fortunately, we find that PMs trained on a
mixture of both datasets can nevertheless learn the right lessons and behave helpfully when appropriate,
while encouraging the polite refusal of harmful requests.

claims.text: Larger preference models performed better on both objectives and were less sensitive to the mixture of helpfulness and harmlessness data.
claims.quote:
However, as model size increases,
PMs perform better on both distributions simultaneously and become much more robust to the relative proportions of helpful and harmless training data.

claims.text: Constitutional AI used constitution-guided self-critique and revision to produce supervised training responses.
claims.quote:
We then ask the model to critique its response according to a principle in
the constitution, and then revise the original response in light of the critique. We revise responses repeatedly
in a sequence, where we randomly draw principles from the constitution at each step. Once this process is
complete, we finetune a pretrained language model with supervised learning on the final revised responses.

claims.text: Constitutional AI's reinforcement-learning stage replaced human harmlessness preferences with AI feedback while retaining human helpfulness labels.
claims.quote:
This stage
mimics RLHF, except that we replace human preferences for harmlessness with ‘AI feedback’ (i.e. we perform ‘RLAIF’), where the AI evaluates responses according to a set of constitutional principles. Just as
RLHF distills human preferences into a single preference model (PM), in this stage we distill LM interpretations of a set of principles back into a hybrid5 human/AI PM (as we use human labels for helpfulness, but
only AI labels for harmlessness).

claims.text: In evaluations that preferred less evasive responses when harmlessness was equal, Constitutional AI models achieved less harmful behavior at a given helpfulness level.
claims.quote:
The RL-CAI models trained
with AI feedback learn to be less harmful at a given level of helpfulness. The crowdworkers evaluating these
models were instructed to prefer less evasive responses when both responses were equally harmless; this is
why the human feedback-trained Helpful and HH models do not differ more in their harmlessness scores.

claims.text: Sparrow combined targeted rule and preference judgements with RLHF, improving human preferences and adversarial robustness without eliminating violations.
claims.quote:
We show that by
combining targeted rule judgements and preference judgements with RLHF, we can train a
model that is preferred to baselines based on prompting, reranking or supervised learning alone
(fig. 2). Simultaneously, Sparrow is much more resilient to adversarial attacks by humans than
our baselines, breaking the targeted rule in only 8% of probe conversations.

output.answer: No: in the long-context experiments, models generally used relevant information best at the beginning or end of the context, with worse performance in the middle, even for explicitly long-context models (2307.03172). Extending the context window did not necessarily improve use of information within it. Irrelevant retrieved passages can reduce accuracy below performance without retrieval; random retrieval lowered the evaluated in-context retrieval-augmented model's performance by more than 10 points on average (2310.01558). Such passages can distract models into incorrect answers and disrupt intermediate questions or answers in multi-hop reasoning. These effects can be mitigated: NLI filtering helps but can discard useful evidence, while fine-tuning on mixed relevant and irrelevant contexts improves robustness.

First, a simple baseline that filters out
retrieved passages that do not entail question-answer pairs according to a natural
language inference (NLI) model. This is effective in preventing performance reduction, but at a cost of also discarding relevant passages. Thus, we propose a
method for automatically generating data to fine-tune the language model to properly leverage retrieved passages, including for challenging multi-hop tasks, using
a mix of relevant and irrelevant contexts at training time. We empirically show that
even 1,000 examples suffice to train the model to be robust to irrelevant contexts
while maintaining high performance on examples with relevant ones.

output.answer: Safety training can fail because language modeling and instruction following compete with safety: a prompt can suppress refusal or induce an affirmative opening that the model then continues into an unsafe answer. A second failure mode is mismatched generalization: pretrained capabilities extend to encodings, formats, and contexts that safety training does not cover. Automated attacks exploit these weaknesses by searching for adversarial suffixes that increase the probability of affirmative responses, using greedy gradient-based optimization or feedback from output probabilities. Optimizing across prompts and models can produce transferable attacks against black-box systems, while model-specific adaptation can uncover weaknesses missed by a fixed attack. The R2D2 example shows why robustness to one trained-against prompt structure does not establish robustness to different structures, such as in-context demonstrations.

claims.text: Safety, language modeling, and instruction-following objectives can conflict, allowing prompts to make refusal costly under the other objectives.
claims.quote:
Competing objectives stems from the observation that safety-trained LLMs are typically trained
against multiple objectives that can conflict with each other. Specifically, state-of-the-art LLMs are
trained for language modeling [12], instruction following [41, 7], and safety [38, 7]. This training
can be exploited by crafting prompts that force a choice between either a restricted behavior or a
response that is heavily penalized by the pretraining and instruction following objectives.

claims.text: Safety training may fail to generalize to inputs that the model can nevertheless understand and follow.
claims.quote:
Our second failure mode comes from observing that pretraining is done on a larger and more diverse
dataset than safety training, and thus the model has many capabilities not covered by safety training.
This mismatch can be exploited for jailbreaks by constructing prompts on which pretraining and
instruction following generalize, but the model’s safety training does not.

claims.text: Refusal suppression can shift the initial response away from refusal, after which the language-modeling objective favors continuing the unsafe answer.
claims.quote:
First, the instruction-following training
responds to the instructions and downweights tokens that start typical refusals. Thus, the model
selects tokens that are more likely to begin responses. Once a response is started, the pretraining
objective heavily favors continuing over an abrupt reversal, leading to a full unsafe output.

claims.text: Automated suffix attacks use greedy and gradient-based search to increase the probability of affirmative responses instead of refusals.
claims.quote:
Specifically, our approach finds a suffix that, when
attached to a wide range of queries for an LLM to produce objectionable content, aims
to maximize the probability that the model produces an affirmative response (rather
than refusing to answer). However, instead of relying on manual engineering, our approach automatically produces these adversarial suffixes by a combination of greedy
and gradient-based search techniques, and also improves over past automatic prompt
generation methods.

claims.text: Suffixes optimized across multiple prompts and models can transfer to black-box production models.
claims.quote:
Surprisingly, we find that the adversarial prompts generated by our approach are
highly transferable, including to black-box, publicly released, production LLMs. Specifically, we train an adversarial attack suffix on multiple prompts (i.e., queries asking for
many different types of objectionable content), as well as multiple models (in our case,
Vicuna-7B and 13B). When doing so, the resulting attack suffix induces objectionable content in the public interfaces to ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude, as
well as open source LLMs such as LLaMA-2-Chat, Pythia, Falcon, and others.

claims.text: Adaptive attacks can use output log-probabilities to optimize suffixes through random search, without needing gradients.
claims.quote:
Our main tool consists of a manually designed prompt template—which is used
for all unsafe requests for a given model—enhanced by an adversarial suffix found with random
search (Rastrigin, 1963) when the logprobs of the generated tokens are at least partially accessible. Our approach can be considered simple as it does not require gradient information (Zou et al.,
2023; Geisler et al., 2024), auxiliary LLMs to iteratively optimize the jailbreaks (Chao et al., 2023;
Mehrotra et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024), or multi-turn conversations (Cheng et al., 2024; Russinovich et al., 2024).

claims.text: R2D2's training against request-plus-suffix attacks left a vulnerability to a different structure using in-context learning.
claims.quote:
Motivated
by the fact that R2D2 was trained to refuse a specific prompt structure (i.e., request and adversarial
suffix), we circumvent safety guardrails by using a different prompt structure. We use an in-context
learning prompt (see Table 6 in the appendix), which we found the model to be particularly sensitive
to.

output.answer: LLM agents can improve at inference time by changing the feedback, memories, and reusable skills available to subsequent attempts while keeping model weights fixed. Reflexion turns evaluation signals into verbal lessons, stores them in persistent memory, and conditions later actions on those lessons alongside the current trajectory. Self-Refine repeatedly asks the same model to critique and revise its output, while Voyager uses environment feedback, execution errors, and self-verification to improve executable programs. Voyager also stores and retrieves code skills, allowing later tasks to build on previously acquired behaviors without parameter fine-tuning. Improvement depends on useful feedback: incorrect self-generated tests can mistakenly validate a bad solution and terminate refinement prematurely.

claims.text: Reflexion converts evaluation feedback into textual guidance supplied as context for the next attempt.
claims.quote:
Reflexion converts binary or scalar feedback from the
environment into verbal feedback in the form of a textual summary, which is then added as additional
context for the LLM agent in the next episode.

claims.text: Reflexion uses the current trajectory as short-term memory and stores reflections in long-term memory to inform subsequent decisions.
claims.quote:
In the RL setup, the trajectory history serves as the short-term
memory while outputs from the Self-Reflection model are stored in long-term memory. These two
memory components work together to provide context that is specific but also influenced by lessons
learned over several trials, which is a key advantage of Reflexion agents over other LLM action
choice works.

claims.text: Self-Refine uses the same model to generate feedback and revise its draft repeatedly, requiring no additional training.
claims.quote:
Given an initial output generated by a model M, we pass it back to the same model M to get
feedback. Then, the feedback is passed back to the same model to refine the previously-generated
draft. This process is repeated either for a specified number of iterations or until M determines that
no further refinement is necessary.

claims.text: Self-Refine's improvements arise from iterative feedback and refinement without training the model further.
claims.quote:
In turn, SELF-REFINE provides an effective way to obtain better outputs
from a single model without any additional training, via iterative (self-)feedback and refinement.

claims.text: Voyager combines a reusable executable skill library with feedback-driven program improvement.
claims.quote:
VOYAGER consists of three
key components: 1) an automatic curriculum that maximizes exploration, 2) an
ever-growing skill library of executable code for storing and retrieving complex
behaviors, and 3) a new iterative prompting mechanism that incorporates environment feedback, execution errors, and self-verification for program improvement.

claims.text: Voyager retrieves stored skills using task plans and environment feedback, making prior experience available for later tasks.
claims.quote:
For skill retrieval, we query the skill library with the embedding of self-generated task
plans and environment feedback (Fig. 4, bottom).

claims.text: Voyager acquires skills through black-box model queries without updating model parameters.
claims.quote:
VOYAGER interacts with GPT-4 via blackbox queries, which bypasses the need for
model parameter fine-tuning.

claims.text: Faulty evaluation can stop the learning loop prematurely by accepting an incorrect solution.
claims.quote:
On the
other hand, if an invalid test suite returns a false positive completion (all internal test cases pass
but the implementation is incorrect), the agent will prematurely report an invalid submission.

output.answer: Factual knowledge stored in model parameters can support competitive closed-book question answering: fine-tuned T5 models answered questions without external evidence, with performance improving as model size increased (2002.08910). However, popularity-sensitive evaluations found that parameter memory is competitive mainly for popular facts, while scaling does little to improve memorization of less popular facts (2212.10511). Retrieval complements this weakness: it improves answers about less popular entities, and on POPQA a retrieval-augmented GPT-Neo 2.7B outperformed vanilla GPT-3. Retrieval is not uniformly beneficial, however: on 10% of POPQA questions it changed a correct GPT-3 answer into an incorrect one, associated with poor retrieval quality. These findings support selectively retrieving evidence for less popular facts while relying on parameter memory for well-memorized popular facts, as implemented by Adaptive Retrieval.

claims.text: Retrieval has an advantage for less popular entities, whereas parameter memory is competitive for more popular entities.
claims.quote:
Retrievalaugmented LMs (dashed) outperform LMs’ parametric memory (solid) for less popular entities, while
parametric memory is competitive for more popular entities.

claims.text: Increasing model size mainly improves memorization of popular knowledge and does not appreciably improve long-tail factual memorization in the evaluated models.
claims.quote:
Scaling, on the other hand, mainly
improves memorization of popular knowledge,
and fails to appreciably improve memorization
of factual knowledge in the long tail.

claims.text: On POPQA, retrieval enables a much smaller model to outperform a larger model answering from its parameters alone.
claims.quote:
A much smaller LM (e.g.,
GPT-Neo 2.7B) augmented by the Contriever retrieval results outperforms vanilla GPT-3.

claims.text: Retrieval can introduce errors: it harmed GPT-3 davinci-003 on 10% of POPQA questions, and those cases had particularly low retrieval recall.
claims.quote:
For 10% of questions, retrievalaugmentation causes the LM to incorrectly answer
a question it could otherwise answer correctly. We
found that on those questions, recall@1 is significantly lower than the overall recall@1 (0.14 vs 0.42
overall), indicating that failed retrieval can result
in performance drops.

claims.text: Parameter-only question answering can nevertheless be competitive: fine-tuning pretrained models without external context produced performance that scaled with model size and competed with retrieval-based systems.
claims.quote:
In this short paper, we measure the practical utility of this
approach by fine-tuning pre-trained models to
answer questions without access to any external context or knowledge. We show that this
approach scales with model size and performs
competitively with open-domain systems that
explicitly retrieve answers from an external
knowledge source when answering questions.

claims.text: Adaptive Retrieval operationalizes this complementarity by retrieving below a popularity threshold and relying on parameter memory for more popular entities.
claims.quote:
In particular, we use retrieval for questions
whose popularity is lower than a threshold (popularity threshold), and for more popular entities, do
not use retrieval at all.
